title: The Weaver's Son and the Cape: Basking Ridge, Washington, Athens, and the Colony He Did Not Live to See
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Glasgow, the yarn inspector takes ship
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Brown pp. 9-11); month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: James Finley is born in Glasgow in 1737, trained as a yarn merchant, and rises to inspector of the yarn factories of the city. John Witherspoon, bound for the presidency of the College of New Jersey, invites him across the water; he sails in 1769 and in Princeton he works a loom. He is never ordained. The office he holds in the Presbyterian church there is ruling elder, a layman's chair beside the pulpit rather than in it. Later encyclopedias will promote him to Reverend and hedge his origin between Scotland and Ireland. Brown, who knew the household, gives Glasgow and gives a weaver.
suggested_refs: The yarn factories of Glasgow, inspected by James Finley before his 1769 emigration
sources: Isaac V. Brown, Memoirs of the Rev. Robert Finley, D.D. (New-Brunswick: Terhune & Letson, 1819), pp. 9-11

stops.name: Princeton, the birth in the weaver's house
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Brown p. 14); day and month not recovered from any source reached, including Geni and WikiTree, which returned no usable content; defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: Three years after the crossing, a son is born to James Finley and his wife, whose maiden name Brown writes as Angres. They name him Robert. The town is Princeton, a college village of some hundreds of souls where the loom and the Latin school stand within a walk of each other, and where a ruling elder's boy grows up under the eye of a president of the college. The date the family keeps is the year only. No parish register reached in this search gives the day, and none is invented here to fill it.
stops.quote: Robert Finley was born at Princeton, New-Jersey, A. D. 1772.
stops.quote_source: Isaac V. Brown, Memoirs of the Rev. Robert Finley, D.D. (1819), p. 14
suggested_refs: The Presbyterian church at Princeton, where James Finley served as ruling elder

stops.name: Nassau Hall, entered at eleven
stops.date_confidence: year attested by age (Wikipedia, 'Robert Finley'); term and day unrecorded, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: At eleven the boy is entered in the College of New Jersey, housed under the single great roof of Nassau Hall, which has been a barracks for both armies and is still repairing itself from the war. He is younger than the men he recites with by four or five years. The course is Latin, Greek, moral philosophy, and the Presbyterian divinity that Witherspoon has made the temper of the place. What the record gives is the age and nothing else. No source reached in this search describes the boy himself, his temper or his standing in the class, until he takes his degree four years later.
suggested_refs: Nassau Hall, Princeton, the whole of the College of New Jersey in 1783

stops.name: Nassau Hall, the degree at fifteen
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Wikipedia, 'Robert Finley'); commencement day not recorded in sources reached, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: He takes his degree at fifteen and walks out of the college with no living to go to and no orders to take. What follows is five years of schoolteaching, the ordinary trade of an unplaced graduate: grammar schools, other men's boys, other men's towns. The encyclopedia entry passes over the whole stretch in a clause, and Brown names no town for most of it. One of the five years is spent a long way south of the Delaware, and it is the only one of them he refers back to in later life.
suggested_refs: The 1787 commencement rolls of the College of New Jersey

stops.name: Charleston, the year in the South
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Finley places the year at Charleston in the early part of his life and Brown places his departure from it in autumn 1792; the opening year is inferred, not attested
stops.campa: He teaches a year in Charleston, South Carolina, in a city where the trade in people is conducted openly at the head of the wharves and where the men who employ him hold their households as property. He calls the post lucrative and laborious. He also carries away from it, by his own account written in 1817, a partiality for the South. He is seventeen. When he comes to write a plan for the removal of free Black Americans, twenty-seven years later, the men he sets out to persuade are the men of this coast.
stops.quote: In the early part of my life I spent a year at Charleston, South Carolina, and brought away with me a partiality for the South.
stops.quote_source: Robert Finley, letter of 21 February 1817, printed in Brown, Memoirs, p. 113
suggested_refs: The Charleston schools of the late 1780s and the wharf-head slave market

stops.name: Princeton, theology under Witherspoon
stops.date_confidence: attested to the season (Brown p. 24, autumn 1792); Wikipedia dates the return to 1793 and is a year late; day defaulted
stops.campa: In the autumn of 1792 he gives up the Charleston post, comes home to Princeton, takes the grammar school again, and begins divinity under Witherspoon, who is old and nearly blind and still president. The arrangement is the ordinary one of the American Presbyterian church before there are seminaries: a candidate reads with a minister, in the minister's house, out of the minister's books. He is twenty. He has been teaching since he was fifteen and will never entirely stop.
stops.quote: in the Autumn of 1792, he relinquished his lucrative and laborious station in Charleston; returned to his native place; resumed the instruction of the grammar school in Princeton; and commenced the study of theology under the superintendence of the venerable President of Nassau Hall.
suggested_refs: John Witherspoon's household at Tusculum, near Princeton, where candidates read divinity
sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert Finley' (dating the return to 1793; contradiction recorded)

stops.name: Nassau Hall, the tutorship
stops.date_confidence: inferred: Brown says the tutorship followed very soon after the autumn 1792 return, without a date; 1793 is a placeholder
stops.campa: Witherspoon and Samuel Stanhope Smith recommend him jointly, and the college takes him as tutor. He hears recitations in the rooms he recited in six years earlier, and reads divinity in the evenings with the president who taught him. From this year he is never only one thing. He is a candidate under care for the ministry and a schoolmaster in the same week, and he is still both in the year he dies. Brown gives the tutorship no date and no term, and no college record fixing either was reached in this search.
suggested_refs: The tutors' rooms of Nassau Hall in the presidency of Samuel Stanhope Smith

stops.name: New Brunswick, licensed to preach
stops.date_confidence: day attested (Brown p. 28); the meeting place is not named in any source reached, and this pin is the presbytery's nominal town, not an attested venue. Presbyteries of this period sat by rotation in member congregations
stops.campa: The Presbytery of New Brunswick licenses him to preach on the sixteenth of September, 1794. Where it sits that day the record does not say, and the presbytery has no fixed house: it meets where its ministers live, at Allentown, at Basking Ridge, wherever the roll is called next. So the town stands here for a body rather than a building, and the pin is an approximation with its reason attached. From the licensure he is a probationer, preaching on trial in other men's pulpits, waiting for a congregation to call him.
suggested_refs: The minute books of the Presbytery of New Brunswick, 1794

stops.name: Basking Ridge, ordained and installed
stops.date_confidence: attested (Brown pp. 29-30): the presbytery met at Basking Ridge on 16 June 1795 and ordained and installed him on the following day
stops.campa: The presbytery meets at Basking Ridge on the sixteenth of June and on the following day ordains him and installs him over the congregation. He is twenty-three. The meeting house he preaches in is not the Greek Revival church that stands on the ground now, which is raised in 1839 and enlarged in 1869; what survives from his time is the churchyard and its oak. He holds this pulpit twenty-two years, until a presbytery unmakes the relation in another town. The count of nineteen years that circulates in the reference works is arithmetic, and it is wrong.
suggested_refs: The Basking Ridge churchyard and its oak, the surviving fabric of Finley's parish

stops.name: Elizabethtown, the Caldwell marriage
stops.date_confidence: month attested (Brown p. 31); day unrecorded. The venue is unattested: this pin stands for the bride's family town, not for a documented church, and a tradition dating the wedding to 1794-1795 is wrong by three or four years
stops.campa: In May 1798 he marries Esther Caldwell, daughter of the Reverend James Caldwell of Elizabethtown, the fighting parson whose church the loyalists burned in 1780 and who was himself shot dead in 1781. The marriage comes three years after the installation, not before it. It also gives him a brother-in-law: Elias Boudinot Caldwell, Clerk of the Supreme Court of the United States, who keeps a house in Washington. Eighteen years on, that house is where he lodges through the five weeks in which he assembles the meeting, and Caldwell is the man who speaks for the plan from the floor of it.
suggested_refs: The Caldwell family of Elizabethtown, New Jersey, and the burned church of 1780
sources: Wikipedia, 'American Colonization Society' (naming the contact John Caldwell; corrected to Elias B. Caldwell)

stops.name: Basking Ridge, a small number of boys
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Brown says soon after the 1795 settlement and gives no date; 1796 is a placeholder for an accretion, not an event
stops.campa: Soon after his settlement he is induced to take on the instruction of a small number of boys. There is no charter and no founding day, only a minister with a parlour and a reputation for Latin. The boys multiply. Within a few years the parlour is a school, and the school draws sons from Virginia and from New York City to a village in the Somerset hills. Brown, counting the whole run, says twenty years and claims no classical seminary on the continent surpassed it. The encyclopedia calls this a re-establishment; nothing in Brown says a school stood here before him.
suggested_refs: The Basking Ridge Classical School in its first, unhoused years

stops.name: Nassau Hall, elected trustee
stops.date_confidence: year attested (Brown p. 54); day of election not recorded in sources reached
stops.campa: The college that took him at eleven puts him on its board at thirty-four, and he holds the trusteeship until he leaves New Jersey altogether. The board governs the one institution that supplies the American Presbyterian church with most of its ministers, and its members are clergymen and lawyers drawn from Georgia to New England. Brown records the election and gives not one line of what Finley did in the seat. Ten years later he walks into Washington carrying a pamphlet and this title.
suggested_refs: The Board of Trustees minutes of the College of New Jersey, 1806-1817

stops.name: Basking Ridge, the brick academy raised
stops.date_confidence: year attested (National Register of Historic Places record for the Brick Academy); month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: He organizes the money and oversees the building: two storeys of brick, put up in 1809 for a school that has outgrown every room lent to it. Enrolment has climbed from under a dozen to an average of twenty-five and sometimes forty. The building outlives the school and the pastor both, and stands in Basking Ridge still, on the National Register. It is the only structure any source reached in this search credits to Robert Finley, and he raised it for a Latin school in a village of a few hundred people.
suggested_refs: The Brick Academy, Basking Ridge, listed on the National Register of Historic Places
sources: National Register of Historic Places record, Brick Academy, Basking Ridge, New Jersey

stops.name: Somerville, the county clerk's book
stops.date_confidence: undated: the New Jersey Slavery Records project cites Somerset County Clerk's Office documents without a date reachable in this search, and the record images were not retrieved; 1810 is a placeholder inside the pastorate. Recorded as reconstruction
stops.campa: In the clerk's office at Somerville lie the county's slavery records, and modern researchers reading them for the founders of the American Colonization Society find Robert Finley of Bernards Township among the men who held people as property. No timeline, no manumission, no institutional answer to the finding could be confirmed in this search. The claim is set down here at the same weight as it was found, which is secondhand, and set down beside the pamphlet rather than away from it.
suggested_refs: New Jersey Slavery Records project, records.njslavery.org, drawing on the Somerset County Clerk's Office
sources: New Jersey Slavery Records project (cited secondhand; record images not retrieved this session)

stops.name: Basking Ridge, the letter of the fourteenth of February
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Brown, Memoirs, p. 17, printing the letter with its date)
stops.campa: Ten months before anyone meets in Washington, the whole scheme is already on a sheet of paper in a country parsonage, written to a private correspondent named John P. Mumford. Finley asks whether the rich and benevolent could not form a colony in Africa on the pattern of Sierra Leone. He writes that the fathers brought them here and the sons are bound to repair the injury. Then he sets down the arithmetic of benefit, and the first term of it is not repair.
stops.quote: Could they be sent back to Africa, a three-fold benefit would arise. We should be cleared of them : - we should send to Africa a population partially civilized and christianized for its benefit : - our blacks themselves would be put in a better situation.
stops.quote_source: Robert Finley to John P. Mumford, Basking Ridge, 14 February 1816, printed in Brown, Memoirs, p. 17
suggested_refs: The Finley-Mumford correspondence of February 1816, printed entire by Brown

stops.name: Off Sierra Leone, the model named in the letter
stops.date_confidence: the date is the letter's, not a visit's: Finley never crossed the Atlantic. The coordinate is the atlas pin for the latitude of Sierra Leone, inherited unchanged from the Columbus journey
stops.campa: The precedent he names is British: Freetown, planted on this coast in 1787 for the poor and freed Black people of London and for loyalist refugees from the American war. He has read of it and reaches for it as a working model, a colony that already exists and can therefore be argued from. This same latitude stands in the atlas already, logged in the Columbus journey, where the third voyage runs south to the line of Sierra Leone to test a theory about equatorial riches. In that stop the parallel is under a keel. In this one it is a line in a letter, written by a man who never crosses the Atlantic.
stops.quote: Could not the rich and benevolent devise means to form a colony on some part of Africa, similar to the one at Sierra Leone, which might gradually induce many free blacks to go and settle, devising for them the means of getting there, and of protection and support, till they were established?
stops.quote_source: Robert Finley to John P. Mumford, 14 February 1816, printed in Brown, Memoirs, p. 17
suggested_refs: The Sierra Leone Company settlement at Freetown, 1787, the working precedent for Liberia
sources: working/journeys/columbus.journey.json (latitude of Sierra Leone, third voyage)

stops.name: Richmond, Mercer and the old debates
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Wikipedia dates Charles Fenton Mercer's advocacy to early 1816 without a day, and Richmond stands here for the Virginia legislature rather than for an attested sitting
stops.campa: In Virginia the legislator Charles Fenton Mercer turns up the record of secret state debates held after Gabriel's rebellion of 1800, in which the Assembly had discussed removing free Black Virginians somewhere beyond the state. He begins arguing for the project in the open. Two men move toward the same object in the same year: a Virginia politician working from the sealed record of a slaveholding state's fear, and a New Jersey minister working from a letter about repairing an injury. Neither knows the other yet.
suggested_refs: The 1800-1805 Virginia Assembly debates on removal, uncovered by Mercer

stops.name: Basking Ridge, Thoughts written before the journey
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: a District eyewitness says the piece was written previous to his coming here, and he arrived about 1 December 1816; November is inferred, not attested
stops.campa: Before he leaves New Jersey he writes the pamphlet out: Thoughts on the Colonization of Free Blacks. It puts two questions at the head, one about what is to be done with free people of colour and one about their happiness consistently with the writer's own, and it answers with a proposal for gradual separation. Brown, printing it three years later, calls it probably the first treatise on the subject published in the United States. Finley carries the manuscript south in his baggage; it is not yet in type, and it will not be set in New Jersey.
suggested_refs: Thoughts on the Colonization of Free Blacks, reprinted entire in Brown, Memoirs, pp. 83-86

stops.name: Washington, arrival with the plan already made
stops.date_confidence: attested to about the first of December (Brown pp. 80-81, eyewitness letter of 10 November 1818); his lodging is not recorded and the pin is the Pennsylvania Avenue ground of the campaign
stops.campa: He reaches the District about the first of December and opens his views to a Washington man who has been contemplating the same object since the previous winter. The encyclopedia account runs the other way: it has Mercer's circle recruiting Finley, who then endorses their plan. Two men who were present tell Brown otherwise. One writes that Finley was the sole mover and promoter of it, and did not leave the District until it was organized. He brings the scheme with him, and spends five weeks putting it into other men's hands.
stops.quote: I know this scheme is from God!
stops.quote_source: Finley in conversation, December 1816, recalled in a Washington eyewitness letter to Brown, 10 November 1818, printed in Brown, Memoirs, p. 82
suggested_refs: The house of Elias Boudinot Caldwell, Clerk of the Supreme Court, in Washington
sources: Wikipedia, 'American Colonization Society' (reversing the causal order; contradiction recorded)

stops.name: The Capitol, calling on the members
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Brown p. 82 records the calls on members of Congress and heads of departments without dates; mid-December is placed between his arrival and the first meeting
stops.campa: Congress is sitting in a Capitol still being rebuilt after the British burned it, and Finley works it like a parish: members of the House, senators, the heads of departments, one after another, a country minister with a pamphlet and a brother-in-law who is Clerk of the Supreme Court. The chamber he walks through is the one Andrew Jackson will enter as a senator six years after Finley is dead, on business that has nothing to do with Africa. Finley is asking every man he meets a question about what the republic owes and what it wants rid of.
suggested_refs: The Fourteenth Congress in session, December 1816, in the rebuilt Capitol

stops.name: The President's House, before Madison
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Brown p. 82 attests that Finley called on President Madison but gives no date; mid-December is inferred
stops.campa: He calls on James Madison, in the last winter of the presidency, in a house rebuilt from its own burning. Madison owns people at Montpelier and will die owning them. Nothing survives of what passes between the two men beyond the fact of the visit, which the Washington eyewitness sets down among the calls Finley made in those weeks. Within four years three presidents who hold slaves, Jefferson and Madison and Monroe, will be counted friends of the society, and the colony's first town will carry the third one's name.
suggested_refs: James Madison's last winter in the President's House, December 1816

stops.name: Washington, the pamphlet set in type
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month: the District correspondent says the piece was reviewed and published there during the campaign, without a day; defaulted to the first of December
stops.campa: The manuscript he carried from New Jersey is reviewed in Washington and printed there, by the men he is recruiting, as campaign material for the meeting he is arranging. So the first American treatise on colonization is published not from a parsonage but from the capital, ten or twenty days before the room is booked. It opens with two questions and answers them as a calculation rather than as a case. The men who read it in Washington in December vote on it in the same month, and the printers of it are the men it was written to persuade.
stops.quote: What shall we do with the free people of colour? What can we do for their happiness consistently with our own?
stops.quote_source: Robert Finley, Thoughts on the Colonization of Free Blacks (Washington, 1816), reprinted in Brown, Memoirs, p. 83
suggested_refs: The Washington printing of Thoughts on the Colonization of Free Blacks, December 1816

stops.name: Davis's Hotel, the meeting of the twenty-first
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Brown pp. 98-99). The building no longer stands and the coordinate approximates its Pennsylvania Avenue site
stops.campa: The room fills on the twenty-first of December: Henry Clay in the chair, John Randolph of Roanoke on his feet, Elias Boudinot Caldwell speaking as a man who has had the plan explained to him across his own table. The meeting does not found anything. It appoints a committee to prepare a constitution and rules for a society to be organized at a subsequent meeting, and adjourns a week. The reference works that date Bushrod Washington's presidency to this evening are reading the minute of the wrong night.
suggested_refs: Davis's Hotel, Pennsylvania Avenue, Washington, site of both December 1816 meetings
sources: Wikipedia, 'American Colonization Society' (dating the officers to 21 December; corrected)

stops.name: Athens, the same day, a chair he does not know of
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: the trustees' resolution is dated at Athens, 21 December 1816 (Brown pp. 109-110)
stops.campa: Six hundred miles south, on the same day, the trustees of the University of Georgia resolve unanimously that the Reverend Robert Finley of New-Jersey be appointed their president in the place of the Reverend John Brown, resigned, at fifteen hundred dollars a year. He is in a Washington hotel room at the time, closing a meeting he has spent five weeks arranging, and knows nothing of it. Governor Peter Early's covering letter will take two months to reach him. Both of the things his name is attached to begin on the twenty-first of December, 1816.
stops.quote: Resolved, That the Rev. Robert Finley, of New-Jersey, be, and he is hereby appointed President of the University of Georgia, in the place of the Rev. John Brown, resigned, with a salary of $1500 per annum.
stops.quote_source: Resolution of the Board of Trustees, Athens, Georgia, 21 December 1816, printed in Brown, Memoirs, pp. 109-110
suggested_refs: The Franklin College trustees' minute book, December 1816
sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert Finley' (dating the acceptance to July 1817; corrected)

stops.name: Davis's Hotel, the constitution adopted
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Brown pp. 98-99). Brown does not name the venue of the adjourned meeting; Davis's Hotel is carried forward from the twenty-first. The Capitol's House chamber belongs to the society's anniversary meetings, the first of them 1 January 1818
stops.campa: On Saturday the twenty-eighth the adjourned meeting sits: citizens of Washington, of Georgetown, of Alexandria and others. The constitution is reported and adopted without a dissenting voice, the American Society for Colonizing the Free People of Colour is completely organized, and officers are appointed for the year. Bushrod Washington, nephew of the first president and a justice of the Supreme Court, takes the chair of it. Finley is made one of the vice-presidents, and on Mr. Herbert's motion closes the meeting with prayer.
stops.quote: On Saturday, 28th of December, 1816, according to adjournment, a large number of citizens of Washington, of Georgetown, of Alexandria, and others, assembled - when Mr. Finley enjoyed the peculiar satisfaction of seeing the expected constitution reported and unanimously adopted.
suggested_refs: The constitution of the American Society for Colonizing the Free People of Colour, adopted 28 December 1816

stops.name: Philadelphia, the alarm among the people of colour
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (Brown pp. 99-100, placing the stop on his January 1817 return); no day given, defaulted to the first
stops.campa: He stops in Philadelphia on the way home and finds the city's Black community already awake to what has been done in Washington and filled, Brown writes, with painful alarms and apprehensions respecting the nature and object of the society. They read removal in it, three weeks after the constitution is signed and before the society owns a ship or a dollar of subscription. He goes among them to quiet the alarm rather than to raise money. Within the month thousands of Black Philadelphians meet and reject the scheme outright.
stops.quote: On his arrival in Philadelphia, he was grieved to find the people of colour in that city filled with painful alarms and apprehensions, respecting the nature and object of the colonization society, so recently instituted at Washington.
suggested_refs: The January 1817 mass meeting of Black Philadelphians against the American Colonization Society

stops.name: Trenton, the auxiliary society
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Brown pp. 99-104 place the New Jersey petition and the auxiliary society's constitution in the winter and spring of 1817 without dates
stops.campa: Home in New Jersey he petitions the legislature and helps constitute a colonization society auxiliary to the one at Washington, with its own constitution and its own officers, at Trenton. This is the whole of his organizing after December: one state, one petition, one auxiliary. The account that has him touring the United States through 1817 for the cause describes a year he did not have, because by late February his correspondence has turned entirely to Georgia and to the question of how a man moves a household eight hundred miles.
suggested_refs: The New Jersey auxiliary colonization society constituted at Trenton, 1817
sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert Finley' (describing national organizing through 1817; corrected)

stops.name: Basking Ridge, the letter of acceptance
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Finley's acceptance is datelined Basking Ridge, Feb. 21, 1817 (Brown p. 113)
stops.campa: Governor Peter Early's letter, written the fifteenth of January and postmarked the twenty-ninth, reaches Basking Ridge on the twentieth of February. He answers the next day. He has never seen Athens, has corresponded with Georgia entirely by post through the Reverend John Hodge and the governor, and accepts a college he knows only as a name and a salary. In the same letter he gives the reason a New Jersey man goes south, and it dates from a schoolroom he left twenty-five years ago.
suggested_refs: Governor Peter Early's letter of 15 January 1817 and Finley's reply, both printed by Brown

stops.name: Allentown, the pastoral relation dissolved
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day: Brown p. 117 quotes the presbytery minute verbatim
stops.campa: The Presbytery of New Brunswick, sitting at Allentown on the twenty-second of April, dissolves the pastoral relation between Robert Finley and the congregation of Basking Ridge. Twenty-two years, one pulpit, one school, one village, closed in a single line of a minute book. The wording is the ordinary wording for a minister translated to a better post; it records no farewell and gives no reason beyond the call. He is forty-five years old, and he has five months and eleven days to live.
suggested_refs: The minute of the Presbytery of New Brunswick at Allentown, 22 April 1817

stops.name: Petersburg, the post road south
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: no itinerary survives. The Virginia post road is the standard route between New Jersey and Georgia in 1817, and the date is inferred from his April release and May arrival
stops.campa: No account of the journey survives, so the road is reconstructed rather than reported: the great post road down through Philadelphia, Baltimore, Richmond and Petersburg, then the Carolina stages, weeks of coach and horse and river ferries with a household in train. He is going toward the country he told Georgia he had a partiality for, on the strength of one year spent teaching in Charleston when he was seventeen. He will not see New Jersey again.
suggested_refs: The southern post road of 1817, Philadelphia to Athens by stage
sources: Reconstruction from period post-road practice; no source reached documents Finley's route

stops.name: Athens, the funds good only in prospect
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (Brown p. 137, arrival in May 1817); day unrecorded
stops.campa: He arrives in May and opens the books. The university's endowment sits in a state bank that opened the previous summer on seventeen per cent of its capital; the money exists as an expectation and not otherwise. What he has been given is not a half-built campus but a solvent-looking institution that is not solvent. He is a schoolmaster of twenty years' standing who has raised one brick building by subscription, and the first thing he does in Georgia is count what is there.
stops.quote: When therefore, Dr. Finley arrived at Athens in May, 1817, he found upon a thorough investigation of the affairs of the institution, that its funds were good only in prospect.
suggested_refs: The Georgia state bank of 1816 and the Franklin College endowment

stops.name: Athens, the summer letters
stops.date_confidence: attested: his Athens letters are dated 12 and 24 June, 1 July and 16 July 1817 (Brown pp. 132-137); this stop stands for the run of them
stops.campa: The letters he writes from Athens in June and July are the letters of a man in good health with work in front of him. He reports on the college, on the students, on the money, and he adds a postscript about the other business, because Washington is five months behind him and still in his hand. A Georgia observer writes afterwards that the success attending the few months of his presidency gave them the most animating hope. Nobody writing that summer treats him as a short-term appointment.
stops.quote: With men of reflection the colonizing scheme is as popular here, as with you in Jersey. Go on and prosper. Be firm and resolute.
stops.quote_source: Robert Finley to an unnamed Brother in New Jersey, from Athens, Georgia, 1817, printed in Brown, Memoirs, p. 132
suggested_refs: Finley's Athens correspondence of June and July 1817

stops.name: Athens, home from the August tour
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the return (Brown); the August tour's route through Georgia is not documented in any source reached
stops.campa: In August he goes out across Georgia to raise money for a college whose endowment is a prospect, and comes home on the eighth of September. The tour is the last work he does. The lines below stand in the same letter that carried the postscript about the colonizing scheme, written in the plain register he keeps for other ministers by a man who has just moved a whole household eight hundred miles into a state where the college's funds are good only in prospect.
stops.quote: Life is short. All flesh is to come a little lower in worldly matters, to rise a little higher in the service of God and man. I have got my personal abasement. Lord grant I may not deserve more.
stops.quote_source: Robert Finley to an unnamed Brother, from Athens, Georgia, 1817, printed in Brown, Memoirs, p. 132
suggested_refs: The August 1817 Georgia subscription tour for Franklin College

stops.name: Athens, the eighteen days
stops.date_confidence: inferred: the contemporary obituary specifies a painful illness of eighteen days, counted back from 3 October 1817
stops.campa: A week after the tour the fever takes him and does not break. Eighteen days, the obituary says, and painful. No source reached in this search names the fever, and Athens in September is a fever town. The claim that he sickened within weeks of arriving is out by three months. He does not reach Georgia and collapse. He works a good summer, rides out to raise money in the August heat, comes home on the eighth of September, and does not get up again. The presidency runs five months, and the last eighteen days of it are spent in a bed.
suggested_refs: The Athens fever season of 1817
sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert Finley' (dating the illness within weeks of arrival; corrected)

stops.name: Athens, death on a Friday morning
stops.date_confidence: attested (contemporary Georgia obituary, Brown p. 153): 3 October 1817 was a Friday, and a letter datelined Washington, Georgia, 14 October already treats the death as a fortnight old. Wikipedia gives 3 November 1817, which fell on a Monday; recorded here as an error rather than as an open dispute
stops.campa: He dies on the morning of Friday the third of October, forty-five years old, five months into the presidency, ten months after the meeting at Davis's Hotel, and one year and eight months after the letter to Mumford. The colony has no name yet, no ship, no ground. What exists of it is a constitution, a list of officers, a pamphlet, and the alarm of the people of Philadelphia. Everything else that will be laid at his door happens after he is in the earth.
stops.quote: Died on Friday Morning, the 3d inst. the Rev. Robert Finley, D.D. President of the University of Georgia, after a painful illness of eighteen days.
stops.quote_source: Contemporary Georgia obituary, reprinted in Brown, Memoirs, p. 153
suggested_refs: The Georgia obituary of October 1817, reprinted by Brown

stops.name: Jackson Street Cemetery, the town burying ground
stops.date_confidence: place attested; the day of burial is not recorded and follows the obituary. Three conflicting coordinates for this grave circulated in the working pool and are reconciled here to the authoritative value
stops.campa: They bury him in the ground Athens has used as its town cemetery since about 1810 and will use until 1856. It is not a campus plot chosen for a college president; it is the public burying ground, and the university grows around it afterwards until the graves stand in the middle of North Campus. The inscription cannot be read here: the memorial page that would carry it returns a refusal to the search, and no photograph of the stone was obtained. What the stone says is a gap. Who paid to cut it is not, and that is settled nine weeks later in a boardroom.
suggested_refs: Jackson Street Cemetery, Athens, in use as the town burying ground c. 1810-1856
sources: Find a Grave memorial 7717 (HTTP 403 Forbidden; inscription unverified)

stops.name: Athens, the trustees vote two hundred dollars
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Brown pp. 166-167, quoting the resolution)
stops.campa: On the twelfth of December, nine days short of a year after appointing him, the board appropriates two hundred dollars for a tombstone over his grave. Asked to educate his eldest son at the college's charge, they resolve instead to educate all of his sons, and give Mrs Finley her choice of two town lots in Athens. The institution he served for five months pays for his headstone and his children's schooling. No source reached in this search names any other monument to him anywhere.
stops.quote: for the purpose of erecting over his grave a suitable tomb-stone, commemorative of his worth and services
stops.quote_source: Resolution of the Board of Trustees of Franklin College, 12 December 1817, printed in Brown, Memoirs, pp. 166-167
suggested_refs: The trustees' resolution of 12 December 1817 on the tombstone and the education of Finley's sons

stops.name: New Brunswick, Terhune and Letson print the Memoirs
stops.date_confidence: year attested from the imprint; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: Isaac V. Brown, who knew him, gathers the letters and the minutes and the pamphlet and prints them at New Brunswick two years after the death, with brief sketches of some of his cotemporaries and numerous notes. Almost everything that can be checked about Robert Finley can be checked here, and almost everything the reference works get wrong about him is wrong because they did not open it. Brown prints, among the letters, a request from a Washington man that history be made to remember who moved first.
stops.quote: If this colony should ever be formed in Africa, great injustice will be done to Mr. Finley, if in the history of it his name be not mentioned as the first mover, and if some town or district in the colony be not called Finley.
stops.quote_source: Washington eyewitness to Isaac V. Brown, 10 November 1818, printed in Brown, Memoirs, pp. 82-83
suggested_refs: Isaac V. Brown, Memoirs of the Rev. Robert Finley, D.D. (New-Brunswick: Terhune & Letson, 1819)
sources: Brown, Memoirs, title page and pp. 82-83

stops.name: Port of New York, the Elizabeth sails
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day (Wikipedia, 'American Colonization Society')
stops.campa: Two years and four months after the death, the ship Elizabeth clears New York with eighty-six free Black Americans aboard, bound for the West African coast: the first voyage the society sends. The common phrasing that this came three years after Finley died is arithmetic done from the wrong death date. Of the passengers and the agents who go with them, many will be dead of fever within months of landfall, and the survivors will be moved twice before there is any ground that holds.
suggested_refs: The voyage of the Elizabeth, New York to West Africa, February 1820

stops.name: Cape Mesurado, the cape taken from King Peter
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month (December 1821, standard Liberia-founding chronology); day of the cession varies between accounts and is not fixed here
stops.campa: Lieutenant Robert Stockton and the society's agent Eli Ayres come to the cape in December 1821 and obtain it from King Peter, by an account no source reached calls voluntary; Stockton conducts the negotiation with a pistol at hand. This is the ground. Four years after Finley dies in Athens, the plan he carried into Washington becomes a stretch of the West African coast, taken in the manner his pamphlet had specified as fair and honourable purchase from the natives.
stops.quote: To colonize them in Africa, would be a much more arduous undertaking. The country must be explored, and some situation chosen, fertile and healthy - expense must be incurred, in fair and honourable purchase from the natives ...
stops.quote_source: Robert Finley, Thoughts on the Colonization of Free Blacks (Washington, 1816), reprinted in Brown, Memoirs, p. 85
suggested_refs: The December 1821 cession of Cape Mesurado by King Peter to Stockton and Ayres

stops.name: Monrovia, the settlers move onto the cape
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day for the move onto the cape; the name Monrovia is applied later in 1822 and Liberia later still, and the three acts are not collapsed here
stops.campa: On the seventh of January 1822 the settlers move onto the cape, and regular emigration begins from that date and runs through the Civil War, carrying more than fifteen thousand free and freed Black Americans out of the United States. The town takes the name of a sitting slaveholding president. The country that grows from it is the ground of the atlas's Liberian journeys: Milton Blahyi is born, fights and preaches inside this state, and every stop of his life sits on ground the society took at Cape Mesurado.
suggested_refs: The settlement of Cape Mesurado, 7 January 1822, and the naming of Monrovia

stops.name: Monrovia, the count of 1843
stops.date_confidence: year attested for the census figure (Wikipedia, 'American Colonization Society'); month and day not applicable, defaulted to January 1
stops.campa: Between 1820 and 1843 about four thousand five hundred and seventy-one emigrants land. In 1843 about one thousand eight hundred and nineteen are recorded alive, some forty in every hundred. The pamphlet had asked whether the establishment would be productive of general happiness and had answered that the difficulties were real and not insurmountable. This is the ledger of the difficulty, and the society keeps it itself. The Black Philadelphians who met in January 1817 argue against the scheme twenty-six years before any of these figures exist.
suggested_refs: The American Colonization Society's own mortality figures for Liberia, 1820-1843

stops.name: Philadelphia, the papers at Lombard Street
stops.date_confidence: undated: the Presbyterian Historical Society was founded in 1852 and the accession date of the Finley material is unknown. The finding aid could not be retrieved (history.pcusa.org redirects to a page returning 404), so the contents rest on a single secondhand citation
stops.campa: What survives of him in manuscript is said to be here, at the Presbyterian Historical Society: sermons, and a manuscript in Latin. The finding aid that would list them redirects to a page that is gone, so the holding is named on one citation and no more. The city is the same city where the people the plan was written about told him to his face what they thought of it, thirty-five years earlier and about a mile from this address. Both records are kept in Philadelphia.
suggested_refs: Presbyterian Historical Society, 425 Lombard Street, Philadelphia, Guide to the Robert Finley Papers (finding aid unreachable)
sources: Wikipedia, 'Robert Finley', citing Presbyterian Historical Society holdings (finding aid 404; contents unverified)

stops.name: Harlem, the return proposed on other terms
stops.date_confidence: the August 1920 convention date is attested for Marcus Garvey; the linkage to Finley is the atlas's own framing and is reconstruction, not a documented descent
stops.campa: A century after the letter to Mumford, Marcus Garvey fills a hall in Harlem and argues a return to Africa that no white society organizes, funds, or supervises, and that no one describes as being cleared of anybody. The atlas queue records the inversion in its own hand: Pan-Africanism preached a hundred years after Finley's colonization movement, on wholly self-determined terms. Garvey's ships are Black-owned and Black-crewed. The Liberia he proposes to settle is the one the society made with white subscriptions a century before, and no source reached in this search records Garvey setting foot in it.
suggested_refs: The 1920 UNIA convention in Harlem and the Black Star Line's Liberia programme
sources: working/journeys/QUEUE.md, line 229 (queue annotation naming the Finley-Garvey inversion)
